platforms.title: Your Contact Lens Habit Might Be Causing Pink Eye
platforms.meta_description: Red, itchy eyes with discharge aren't just bad luck. How you handle contacts and share towels can directly determine how conjunctivitis spreads.
platforms.body_html:
Red, itchy eyes with crusty discharge get blamed on allergies or bad luck, but bacterial and viral conjunctivitis — commonly called pink eye — spreads through specific everyday habits far more than random chance.

How the Infection Actually Travels

The conjunctiva is the thin, clear membrane covering the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. When bacteria or a virus reaches it, inflammation follows, and according to the CDC, both viral and bacterial conjunctivitis are highly contagious — spread mainly through direct or indirect contact with the fluid that drains from an infected eye. That's why three specific habits do most of the work in keeping an infection circulating rather than letting it clear.

Touching or rubbing the eyes frequently is the most direct route: once a hand picks up discharge from an infected eye, touching the same or the other eye again reintroduces the bacteria or virus right back where it can keep multiplying. Sleeping in contact lenses or not cleaning them properly is a separate risk — bacteria that build up on a lens surface sit directly against the conjunctiva for hours, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology specifically warns that sleeping in lenses raises infection risk regardless of how the lenses are labeled. Sharing towels or pillowcases is the third: any discharge on the fabric transfers bacteria or virus directly to the next person's eyes and skin, which is also why swimming pools and shared washcloths are common outbreak sources in the CDC's guidance.

What Actually Stops the Spread

  • Wash your hands before touching your eyes, every time, not just when they feel irritated — this breaks the most common transmission route on its own.
  • Always remove contact lenses before sleeping, and clean them with fresh solution daily rather than topping off old solution in the case.
  • Use your own towel and pillowcase during an active infection, and wash them in hot water afterward rather than reusing them straight away.
  • See a doctor if symptoms include eye pain, light sensitivity, or blurred vision rather than just redness and discharge — those additional symptoms can signal a different, more serious eye condition that needs prompt treatment.

According to the CDC, acute conjunctivitis affects roughly 3 to 6 million people every year in the United States alone, making it one of the most common eye conditions doctors see. Viral conjunctivitis tends to affect adults more often, while bacterial conjunctivitis is more common in children, which is part of why it spreads so easily through households and classrooms once one person picks it up.

Viral conjunctivitis often clears on its own within one to two weeks, while bacterial cases may need antibiotic drops from a doctor — but regardless of which type it is, most people remain contagious as long as their eyes are actively watering or producing discharge, according to CDC guidance, which is the real reason hand-washing and not sharing towels matter as much in the first few days as any treatment does.
